chapter_sections.label: DEFINITION:
chapter_sections.text: A CHEMICAL REACTION is a process in which the nature and identity of the initial substances change. New substances with different properties are formed. The substances that undergo change are called REACTANTS and the new substances formed are called PRODUCTS.

chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A chemical reaction has taken place when we observe: change in state, change in colour, evolution of a gas, or change in temperature.
Chemical reactions occur all around us: souring of milk, rusting of iron, fermentation of grapes, digestion of food, respiration.
A chemical reaction involves breaking of old bonds and making of new bonds between atoms.
A chemical equation is a short and concise way to represent a chemical reaction.
Chemical equations must be balanced to satisfy the LAW OF CONSERVATION OF MASS: mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction.
Physical states in equations: (g) = gas, (l) = liquid, (aq) = aqueous solution, (s) = solid.
Reaction conditions (heat, light, catalyst) are written above or below the arrow.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: A CHEMICAL EQUATION is a symbolic representation of a chemical reaction using chemical formulae of the reactants and products. A WORD-EQUATION is a longer form that uses the names of substances. A chemical equation is shorter and more informative than a word-equation.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: In a word-equation, reactants are written on the LEFT-HAND SIDE (LHS) and products on the RIGHT-HAND SIDE (RHS) separated by an arrow (->).
A plus sign (+) is used between multiple reactants and between multiple products.
The arrowhead points towards the products and shows the direction of the reaction.
A SKELETAL CHEMICAL EQUATION uses chemical formulae but is not balanced (unequal atoms on LHS and RHS).
A chemical equation must be balanced so that the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides.
Example word-equation: Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium oxide.
Example chemical equation: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 1.1:
sections.aim: To observe burning of magnesium ribbon and identify it as a chemical reaction.
sections.materials: Magnesium ribbon (3-4 cm), sandpaper, tongs, spirit lamp/burner, watch-glass.
procedure: 1. Clean a magnesium ribbon about 3-4 cm long by rubbing with sandpaper.
2. Hold it with a pair of tongs.
3. Burn it using a spirit lamp or burner; collect the ash in a watch-glass (Fig. 1.1).
4. Keep the burning ribbon away from the eyes. CAUTION: Teacher's assistance needed; wear eyeglasses.
sections.observation: The magnesium ribbon burns with a dazzling white flame and changes into a white powder (magnesium oxide).
sections.conclusion:
A chemical reaction has occurred. Magnesium reacted with oxygen to form magnesium oxide.
Word-equation: Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium oxide.
Chemical equation: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 1.2:
sections.aim: To observe a chemical reaction between lead nitrate and potassium iodide solutions.
sections.materials: Lead nitrate solution, potassium iodide solution, test tube.
procedure: 1. Take lead nitrate solution in a test tube.
2. Add potassium iodide solution to it.
3. Observe.
sections.observation: A yellow precipitate is formed immediately.
sections.conclusion:
A chemical reaction (double displacement/precipitation) has taken place. Yellow lead iodide precipitate is formed.
Equation: Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 1.3:
sections.aim: To observe the reaction between zinc and dilute sulphuric acid.
sections.materials: Zinc granules, conical flask/test tube, dilute hydrochloric acid or sulphuric acid.
procedure: 1. Take a few zinc granules in a conical flask or test tube.
2. Add dilute HCl or H2SO4 (handle with care, Fig. 1.2).
3. Observe around the zinc granules.
4. Touch the conical flask - note any temperature change.
sections.observation: Bubbles form around zinc granules; the flask becomes warm.
sections.conclusion:
A chemical reaction has taken place. Hydrogen gas is evolved; temperature increases.
Word-equation: Zinc + Sulphuric acid -> Zinc sulphate + Hydrogen.
Chemical equation: Zn(s) + H2SO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g).

items.question: What is a word-equation? Write the word-equation for Activity 1.1.
items.answer:
A WORD-EQUATION is a representation of a chemical reaction using the names of reactants and products. Reactants are written on the left and products on the right of an arrow (->).
Word-equation for Activity 1.1: Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium oxide.

items.question: What is a skeletal chemical equation? Give one example and explain why it needs to be balanced.
items.answer:
A SKELETAL CHEMICAL EQUATION is a chemical equation written using chemical formulae but in which the number of atoms of each element is not equal on both sides (LHS not equal to RHS).
Example: Mg + O2 -> MgO (skeletal - unbalanced; 2 O atoms on LHS, 1 on RHS).
It needs to be balanced to satisfy the law of conservation of mass - atoms cannot be created or destroyed.

items.question: What information does a complete chemical equation with state symbols convey? Give one example showing all features.
items.answer:
A complete chemical equation with state symbols conveys:
(i) Names and formulae of all reactants and products.
(ii) Physical states of each substance: (g) gas, (l) liquid, (aq) aqueous, (s) solid.
(iii) Ratio of moles (number of molecules) of each substance.
(iv) Reaction conditions (temperature, catalyst) written above or below the arrow.
Example: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -[Heat]-> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g).
This tells us: solid iron reacts with steam (gaseous water) on heating to give solid iron(II,III) oxide and hydrogen gas; ratio 3:4:1:4.

items.explanation: Reactants are always on the LHS and products on the RHS of the arrow. Options A, C, D are incorrect positions for reactants.

items.explanation: This uses chemical formulae but is unbalanced (2 O on LHS, 1 O on RHS). An unbalanced formula-equation is called a skeletal equation.

items.explanation: (aq) = aqueous (dissolved in water). (g) = gas, (l) = liquid, (s) = solid.

items.explanation: Law of conservation of mass states mass is neither created nor destroyed, so total atoms of each element must be equal on both sides.

items.question: The balanced equation for the reaction of iron with steam is:
items.explanation: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2. Check: Fe:3=3, H:8=8, O:4=4. Balanced. This is the correct balanced equation for iron reacting with steam.

items.question: In Activity 1.3, the temperature of the flask rises because:

options.B: Zinc reacts with H2SO4 releasing heat (exothermic reaction)
options.D: The acid heats up when poured

items.explanation: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2 is an exothermic displacement reaction. Heat is released, making the flask warm. This is a sign of chemical reaction.

items.explanation: Al + Cl2 -> AlCl3. Cl: LCM of 2 and 3 = 6. Need 3 Cl2 and 2 AlCl3: Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3. Balance Al: 2Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3. Check: Al:2=2, Cl:6=6. Coefficients = 2,3,2.

items.question: In Activity 1.2, when lead nitrate and potassium iodide solutions are mixed, which observation confirms a chemical reaction?
items.explanation: Formation of a yellow precipitate (PbI2) from two colourless solutions is the sign of chemical reaction. This is a change in colour/state indicating a double displacement reaction.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: WRITING A CHEMICAL EQUATION means converting a word-equation into a shorter symbolic form by replacing the names of substances with their chemical formulae. The result (before balancing) is called a SKELETAL CHEMICAL EQUATION.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Replace each substance name with its correct chemical formula.
Keep the arrow (->) between reactants (LHS) and products (RHS).
Use + between multiple reactants and between multiple products.
Reaction conditions (heat, light, catalyst) are written above or below the arrow.
A skeletal equation may be unbalanced - it only shows formulae, not correct atom ratios.
Example: "Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium oxide" becomes Mg + O2 -> MgO (skeletal).
Example: "Zinc + Sulphuric acid -> Zinc sulphate + Hydrogen" becomes Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2 (already balanced).
Example with conditions: CO(g) + 2H2(g) -[340 atm]-> CH3OH(l).
Example with catalyst: 6CO2(aq) + 12H2O(l) -[Sunlight/Chlorophyll]-> C6H12O6(aq) + 6O2(aq) + 6H2O(l).

items.question: Convert the following word-equation into a skeletal chemical equation: Zinc + Silver nitrate -> Zinc nitrate + Silver.
items.answer:
Replacing names with formulae:
Zinc = Zn, Silver nitrate = AgNO3, Zinc nitrate = Zn(NO3)2, Silver = Ag.
Skeletal equation: Zn + AgNO3 -> Zn(NO3)2 + Ag.
(Note: This is unbalanced. Balanced: Zn + 2AgNO3 -> Zn(NO3)2 + 2Ag.)

items.question: What is the difference between a word-equation and a chemical equation? Write both forms for the burning of magnesium.
items.answer:
WORD-EQUATION: Uses names of substances. Longer form. Cannot show number of atoms. Cannot be balanced.
Example: Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium oxide.

CHEMICAL EQUATION: Uses chemical formulae. Shorter and more concise. Shows number of atoms and their ratios. Can be balanced.
Example: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s).

Key difference: A chemical equation uses symbols/formulae; a word-equation uses names. Chemical equations can represent atom ratios; word-equations cannot.

items.question: Write skeletal chemical equations for the following, then identify which are already balanced:
items.answer:
(i) Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2.
Check: Na:1=1, H:2 vs 3, O:1=1. NOT balanced (H unequal).
Balanced: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2.

(ii) Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2.
Check: Zn:1=1, H:2=2, S:1=1, O:4=4. ALREADY BALANCED.

(iii) H2 + Cl2 -> HCl.
Check: H:2 vs 1, Cl:2 vs 1. NOT balanced.
Balanced: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl.

Equation (ii) is already balanced. Equations (i) and (iii) need balancing.

items.explanation: Mg has valency 2 and O has valency 2, so they combine in 1:1 ratio giving MgO. Other options do not satisfy valency rules.

items.question: In a chemical equation, the arrow (->) indicates:

options.A: The reaction goes from products to reactants
options.B: The reaction goes from reactants to products

items.explanation: The arrow points from reactants (LHS) to products (RHS), showing direction of the reaction. A double arrow indicates reversibility.

items.question: The skeletal equation for reaction of iron with steam is:
items.explanation: Iron reacts with steam to form iron(II,III) oxide Fe3O4 and hydrogen gas. The skeletal form (before balancing) is Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2.

items.question: Reaction conditions such as heat or catalyst are written in a chemical equation:

options.B: Inside the arrow or above/below it

items.explanation: Reaction conditions (temperature, pressure, catalyst) are written above or below the arrow in a chemical equation. Example: CaCO3 -[Heat]-> CaO + CO2.

items.question: In the skeletal equation Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2, how many molecules of H2O are needed to balance?
items.explanation: Balanced: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2. Fe3O4 has 4 O atoms, so 4 H2O needed. This gives 8 H atoms on LHS and 8 H atoms (4xH2) on RHS. Hence 4 H2O molecules needed.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: A BALANCED CHEMICAL EQUATION is one in which the number of atoms of each element is equal on both the left-hand side (LHS) and right-hand side (RHS) of the equation. Balancing satisfies the law of conservation of mass.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Only COEFFICIENTS (numbers placed in front of formulae) can be changed to balance an equation.
SUBSCRIPTS (numbers inside formulae) must NEVER be changed - changing subscripts changes the substance itself.
The HIT-AND-TRIAL METHOD: place coefficients by trial to make atom counts equal on both sides.
Balancing steps (example: Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2):
Step I: Draw boxes around each formula.
Step II: List atoms on LHS and RHS.
Step III: Start with compound having maximum atoms (Fe3O4 has 3 Fe and 4 O).
Step IV: Balance O: 4 O in Fe3O4 -> put 4 before H2O.
Step V: Balance H: 4 H2O gives 8 H -> put 4 before H2.
Step VI: Balance Fe: 3 Fe in Fe3O4 -> put 3 before Fe.
Step VII: Add state symbols: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g).
State symbols: (g), (l), (aq), (s) are added after balancing for a complete equation.
Physical states are NOT included unless necessary, unless specified.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (DO YOU KNOW):
sections.text:
A solution of slaked lime (Ca(OH)2) produced from quick lime (CaO) is used for whitewashing walls.
CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + Heat.
Calcium hydroxide slowly reacts with CO2 in air to form calcium carbonate:
Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l).
CaCO3 forms after 2-3 days and gives the shiny finish to whitewashed walls. Importantly, the chemical formula of marble is also CaCO3.

items.question: While balancing a chemical equation, what must NOT be changed and what CAN be changed?
items.answer:
MUST NOT change: Chemical formulae (subscripts inside formulae). Changing a formula changes the substance itself.
CAN change: Coefficients (numbers written in front of formulae). Only coefficients are adjusted to balance the equation.

items.question: Why is a balanced chemical equation more informative than a skeletal equation?
items.answer:
A balanced chemical equation gives:
(i) The exact ratio of moles of reactants and products.
(ii) The total number of atoms of each element on both sides are equal, satisfying the law of conservation of mass.
A skeletal equation shows only the formulae of reactants and products but does not give correct atom ratios and does not satisfy the law of conservation of mass.

items.question: Balance step by step: Al + Cl2 -> AlCl3.
items.answer:
Step 1 - List atoms: LHS: Al=1, Cl=2. RHS: Al=1, Cl=3.
Step 2 - Balance Cl: LCM of 2 and 3 = 6. Put 3 before Cl2, 2 before AlCl3:
Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3. Cl: LHS=6, RHS=6. Balanced.
Step 3 - Balance Al: RHS has 2 Al. Put 2 before Al:
2Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3. Al: LHS=2, RHS=2. Balanced.
Final with state symbols: 2Al(s) + 3Cl2(g) -> 2AlCl3(s).
Verification: Al:2=2, Cl:6=6. Fully balanced.

items.question: What is the hit-and-trial method of balancing equations? Using this method, balance: HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(NO3)2 + H2O.
items.answer:
HIT-AND-TRIAL METHOD: Coefficients (whole numbers) are placed in front of chemical formulae by trial until the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides. No subscripts are changed.

Balancing HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(NO3)2 + H2O:
Step 1: List atoms. LHS: H=1+2=3, N=1, O=3+2=5, Ca=1. RHS: Ca=1, N=2, O=6+1=7, H=2.
Step 2: Balance Ca: 1=1. Already balanced.
Step 3: Balance N: Ca(NO3)2 has 2 N. Put 2 before HNO3:
2HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(NO3)2 + H2O. N: 2=2.
Step 4: Balance H: LHS=2+2=4, RHS=2 (in H2O). Put 2 before H2O:
2HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O. H: 4=4.
Step 5: Check O: LHS=6+2=8, RHS=6+2=8. Balanced.
Final: 2HNO3(aq) + Ca(OH)2(aq) -> Ca(NO3)2(aq) + 2H2O(l).
Verification: H:4=4, N:2=2, O:8=8, Ca:1=1. Fully balanced.

items.question: Write balanced chemical equations with state symbols for:
items.answer:
(i) NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + H2O.
Balance Na: Na2SO4 has 2 Na. Put 2 before NaOH: 2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + H2O.
Balance H: LHS=2+2=4, RHS=2. Put 2 before H2O: 2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O.
Check: Na:2=2, O:2+4=6=4+2=6, H:4=4, S:1=1. Balanced.
Final: 2NaOH(aq) + H2SO4(aq) -> Na2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l).

(ii) BaCl2 + H2SO4 -> BaSO4 + HCl.
Balance Cl: 2 Cl on LHS. Put 2 before HCl: BaCl2 + H2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2HCl.
Check: Ba:1=1, Cl:2=2, H:2=2, S:1=1, O:4=4. Balanced.
Final: BaCl2(aq) + H2SO4(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2HCl(aq).

items.question: State the law of conservation of mass. Using the balanced equation 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, show how the law is satisfied. Also write balanced equations for the following and verify: (i) N2 + H2 -> NH3 (ii) NaCl + AgNO3 -> AgCl + NaNO3.
items.answer:
LAW OF CONSERVATION OF MASS: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.

Verification for 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s):
Atoms on LHS: Mg=2, O=2 (from O2).
Atoms on RHS: Mg=2 (in 2MgO), O=2 (in 2MgO).
Mg: 2=2. O: 2=2. All atoms accounted for. No atom created or destroyed. Law satisfied.
Mass: 2x24 + 32 = 80 g (LHS) = 2x40 = 80 g (RHS).

(i) N2 + H2 -> NH3.
N: 2 on LHS, 1 in NH3. Put 2 before NH3: N2 + H2 -> 2NH3.
H: 2 on LHS, 6 in 2NH3. Put 3 before H2: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3.
Verification: N:2=2, H:6=6. Balanced. Law satisfied.

(ii) NaCl + AgNO3 -> AgCl + NaNO3.
Check: Na:1=1, Cl:1=1, Ag:1=1, N:1=1, O:3=3. Already balanced.
Final: NaCl(aq) + AgNO3(aq) -> AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq).
Verification: All atoms equal on both sides. Law satisfied.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Chemical reactions can be CLASSIFIED into types based on how atoms are rearranged, how many reactants and products are involved, and the nature of changes occurring. The five main types studied here are: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, and oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: COMBINATION: Two or more substances combine to form ONE single product. A + B -> AB.
DECOMPOSITION: ONE substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances. AB -> A + B. (Opposite of combination.)
DISPLACEMENT: More reactive element displaces less reactive element from its compound. A + BC -> AC + B.
DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT: Two compounds exchange ions to form two new compounds. AB + CD -> AD + CB.
OXIDATION: Gain of oxygen OR loss of hydrogen by a substance.
REDUCTION: Loss of oxygen OR gain of hydrogen by a substance.
REDOX: Oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously in the same reaction.
EXOTHERMIC: Heat is released along with products.
ENDOTHERMIC: Energy is absorbed (heat, light, or electricity needed).
Decomposition reactions are endothermic; combination reactions are often exothermic.

items.question: What is the difference between a combination reaction and a decomposition reaction? Give one equation for each.
items.answer:
COMBINATION: Two or more reactants combine to form a single product.
Example: CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + Heat.
DECOMPOSITION: One reactant breaks down into two or more products.
Example: CaCO3(s) -[Heat]-> CaO(s) + CO2(g).
They are opposite types: combination builds up; decomposition breaks down.

items.question: What are exothermic and endothermic reactions? Give one example of each.
items.answer:
EXOTHERMIC: A reaction in which heat is released along with products.
Example: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(g) + Heat. (Burning of natural gas.)
ENDOTHERMIC: A reaction in which energy is absorbed.
Example: Ba(OH)2 + 2NH4Cl -> BaCl2 + 2NH3 + 2H2O. (Mixture becomes cold - heat absorbed.)

items.question: Define displacement reaction with the help of Activity 1.9. Write the balanced equation observed.
items.answer:
DISPLACEMENT REACTION: A reaction in which a MORE REACTIVE element displaces a LESS REACTIVE element from its compound in solution.
Activity 1.9: Iron nails placed in copper sulphate solution for 20 minutes.
Observations:
(i) Blue colour of CuSO4 solution fades in test tube B (with iron nails).
(ii) Iron nails become brownish (copper deposits on their surface).
Explanation: Iron (more reactive) displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.
Balanced equation: Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s).

items.question: What is a double displacement reaction? Describe Activity 1.10. Write the balanced equation with state symbols and name the precipitate.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: A DECOMPOSITION REACTION is a reaction in which a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances when energy (heat, light, or electricity) is applied. It is the OPPOSITE of a combination reaction. General form: AB -> A + B.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Decomposition reactions ABSORB energy - they are ENDOTHERMIC.

(i) THERMAL DECOMPOSITION: Energy from heat. Example: CaCO3 -[Heat]-> CaO + CO2.
(ii) ELECTROLYTIC DECOMPOSITION: Energy from electricity. Example: 2H2O -[Electricity]-> 2H2 + O2.
(iii) PHOTOCHEMICAL DECOMPOSITION: Energy from light. Example: 2AgCl -[Sunlight]-> 2Ag + Cl2.
In electrolysis of water: H2:O2 = 2:1 by volume (double H2 at cathode, half O2 at anode).
AgCl and AgBr decompose in sunlight - used in black and white photography.
Decomposition of CaCO3 to CaO is used in cement industry.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
A DISPLACEMENT REACTION is a reaction in which a MORE REACTIVE element displaces (removes) a LESS REACTIVE element from its compound in solution. The more reactive element takes the place of the less reactive one.
General form: A + BC -> AC + B (where A is more reactive than B).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Only a more reactive element can displace a less reactive one; NOT vice versa.
Activity 1.9: Iron (more reactive) displaces copper from CuSO4 solution.

Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s) [Fe displaces Cu]
Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s) [Zn displaces Cu]
Pb(s) + CuCl2(aq) -> PbCl2(aq) + Cu(s) [Pb displaces Cu]
Zinc and lead are more reactive than copper; copper cannot displace Fe, Zn, or Pb.

items.question: Define displacement reaction. Write balanced equations for three examples. Which element is displaced in each?

DISPLACEMENT REACTION: A reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound in solution.

Three examples:
(i) Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s). Iron displaces COPPER.
(ii) Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s). Zinc displaces COPPER.

items.question: In Activity 1.9, explain each observation (blue colour fades; nails become brownish) with reference to the chemical reaction. Write the balanced equation.
items.answer:
Chemical reaction: Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s).

Observation 1 - Blue colour fades:
CuSO4 solution is blue due to Cu^2+ ions. As the reaction proceeds, Cu^2+ ions are CONSUMED (converted to Cu metal). FeSO4 (with Fe^2+ ions) is produced. FeSO4 solution is pale green/nearly colourless. So as [Cu^2+] decreases, blue colour fades.

Observation 2 - Iron nails become brownish:
As Cu^2+ is displaced from solution, COPPER METAL (Cu) deposits on the surface of iron nails. Copper metal has a reddish-brown colour. Therefore the iron nails appear brownish due to the copper coating.

Both observations confirm: Iron (more reactive than Cu) has displaced copper from CuSO4 solution. This is a displacement reaction.

sections.label: DEFINITION:

A DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT REACTION is a reaction in which two ionic compounds exchange their IONS (radicals) to form two new compounds. An insoluble precipitate is often formed. These are also called PRECIPITATION REACTIONS.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Two ionic compounds exchange BOTH their positive and negative ions simultaneously.
A PRECIPITATE (insoluble solid) often forms - its state symbol is (s).
Activity 1.10: Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl. White BaSO4 precipitate.
Activity 1.2 (Recall): Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3. Yellow PbI2 precipitate.
The insoluble product is called a precipitate; the reaction is a precipitation reaction.
Difference from displacement: In displacement, ONE element moves; in double displacement, TWO ionic groups (ions) exchange between two compounds.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 1.10:
sections.aim: To observe double displacement reaction between sodium sulphate and barium chloride.
sections.materials: Sodium sulphate solution (3 mL), barium chloride solution (3 mL), two test tubes.
procedure: 1. Take 3 mL sodium sulphate solution in a test tube.
2. Take 3 mL barium chloride solution in another test tube.
3. Mix the two solutions (Fig. 1.9).
4. Observe.
sections.observation: A WHITE PRECIPITATE is immediately formed.
sections.conclusion:
Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq).
White precipitate = BaSO4 (barium sulphate, insoluble). Ba^2+ from BaCl2 combines with SO4^2- from Na2SO4. Na+ and Cl- remain in solution as NaCl. DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT + PRECIPITATION reaction.

items.question: What is a precipitation reaction? Give one example with balanced equation.
items.answer:
A PRECIPITATION REACTION is a type of double displacement reaction in which an INSOLUBLE SOLID (precipitate) forms when two solutions are mixed.
Example: Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq).
White barium sulphate (BaSO4) precipitate forms instantly.

items.question: How is a double displacement reaction different from a displacement reaction? Give one example of each.
items.answer:
DISPLACEMENT REACTION: ONE element displaces another from a compound. Involves an element + compound as reactants.
Example: Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s). Iron (element) displaces copper.

DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT REACTION: TWO ionic compounds exchange their ions to form two new compounds. Both reactants are ionic compounds.
Example: Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq). Sulphate and chloride ions exchange.

Key difference: Displacement = one element moves; Double displacement = ionic compounds exchange ion pairs. Double displacement often produces a precipitate.

items.question: Describe Activity 1.10 and Recall Activity 1.2. Write balanced equations for both. Name the precipitates and their colours.

sections.label: Activity 1.10 - Na2SO4 + BaCl2:
procedure: Add potassium iodide solution to lead nitrate solution.

YELLOW precipitate forms.
Balanced equation: Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq).
Precipitate: PbI2 (lead iodide, YELLOW, insoluble).
Ion exchange: Pb^2+ (from Pb(NO3)2) + I^- (from KI) -> PbI2(s).

Both are double displacement AND precipitation reactions.

items.question: In Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl, the white precipitate is:
items.explanation: BaSO4 (barium sulphate) is insoluble in water - state symbol (s) indicates precipitate. NaCl is soluble (aq). Na2SO4 and BaCl2 are reactants.

items.question: In Activity 1.2, the yellow precipitate formed when Pb(NO3)2 + KI is:
items.explanation: Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 + 2KNO3. LEAD IODIDE (PbI2) is yellow and insoluble = precipitate. KNO3 is soluble.

items.question: In a double displacement reaction, what is exchanged between the two reacting compounds?
items.explanation: In double displacement, IONS (charged groups) are exchanged. Example: SO4^2- and Cl- exchange in Activity 1.10. Not electrons (that would be redox), not protons (acid-base), not just metal atoms.

items.question: Which is a correct example of a double displacement reaction?
items.explanation: AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3: two ionic compounds exchange ions (Ag+ with Na+; NO3^- with Cl^-). AgCl = white precipitate. A = displacement; B = combination; D = decomposition.

items.question: In Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq), which pair of ions forms the precipitate?
items.explanation: PbI2 precipitate = Pb^2+ (from Pb(NO3)2) + I^- (from KI). K+ and NO3^- remain in solution as soluble KNO3. Pb^2+ and NO3^- are together in the reactant Pb(NO3)2 - they don't combine as precipitate.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
OXIDATION: A process in which a substance GAINS OXYGEN or LOSES HYDROGEN.
REDUCTION: A process in which a substance LOSES OXYGEN or GAINS HYDROGEN.
REDOX REACTION: A reaction in which OXIDATION and REDUCTION occur SIMULTANEOUSLY. One substance is oxidised while another is reduced.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: OXIDISING AGENT: The substance that PROVIDES OXYGEN (causes oxidation of another); itself gets REDUCED.
REDUCING AGENT: The substance that PROVIDES HYDROGEN or removes oxygen (causes reduction of another); itself gets OXIDISED.
In CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O: CuO is REDUCED (loses O) = OXIDISING AGENT. H2 is OXIDISED (gains O) = REDUCING AGENT.
Examples of redox reactions:
ZnO + C -> Zn + CO: ZnO reduced, C oxidised.
MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2: MnO2 reduced, HCl oxidised.
4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O: Na oxidised.
Summary rule: GAIN O or LOSE H = OXIDISED. LOSE O or GAIN H = REDUCED.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 1.11:
sections.aim: To observe oxidation of copper and subsequent reduction by hydrogen gas.
sections.materials: Copper powder (1 g), china dish, wire gauze, tripod stand, burner, hydrogen gas supply.
procedure: 1: 2Cu(s) + O2(g) -[Heat]-> 2CuO(s). Cu GAINS O -> Cu is OXIDISED.
Step 2: CuO(s) + H2(g) -[Heat]-> Cu(s) + H2O(l). CuO LOSES O -> CuO is REDUCED. H2 GAINS O -> H2 is OXIDISED.
Redox: CuO = oxidising agent (causes H2 to be oxidised; itself reduced). H2 = reducing agent (causes CuO to be reduced; itself oxidised).

(i) 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O. Na GAINS oxygen -> Na is OXIDISED. O2 is incorporated.
(ii) CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O. CuO LOSES oxygen -> CuO is REDUCED. H2 GAINS oxygen -> H2 is OXIDISED.

items.question: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen gain/loss.
items.answer:
OXIDATION: Gain of oxygen (or loss of hydrogen) by a substance. The substance is oxidised.
REDUCTION: Loss of oxygen (or gain of hydrogen) by a substance. The substance is reduced.
Example: In CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O: CuO loses O (REDUCED); H2 gains O (OXIDISED).

items.question: What is a redox reaction? Give one example with equation.
items.answer:
A REDOX REACTION is one in which OXIDATION and REDUCTION occur simultaneously. One reactant is oxidised while another is reduced.
Example: ZnO(s) + C(s) -> Zn(s) + CO(g).
ZnO loses O -> REDUCED. C gains O -> OXIDISED. Both occur simultaneously = redox.

items.question: Describe Activity 1.11. Write equations for both steps. What does this demonstrate?
items.answer:
Activity 1.11:
Step 1 - Heat copper powder: Surface of copper (brown) becomes coated with BLACK substance.
Equation: 2Cu(s) + O2(g) -[Heat]-> 2CuO(s). Cu gains O -> OXIDISED.

Step 2 - Pass H2 over heated CuO: Black coating turns BROWN (copper restored).
Equation: CuO(s) + H2(g) -[Heat]-> Cu(s) + H2O(l). CuO loses O -> REDUCED. H2 gains O -> OXIDISED.

This demonstrates:
(i) Oxidation = gain of oxygen by copper.
(ii) Reduction = loss of oxygen by CuO.
(iii) Both occur simultaneously in Step 2 = REDOX reaction.
CuO = oxidising agent; H2 = reducing agent.

items.question: Identify oxidised and reduced substances and name oxidising/reducing agents in:
items.answer:
(i) CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O:
CuO: loses O (CuO -> Cu) -> REDUCED. CuO = OXIDISING AGENT.
H2: gains O (H2 -> H2O) -> OXIDISED. H2 = REDUCING AGENT.

(ii) ZnO + C -> Zn + CO:
ZnO: loses O (ZnO -> Zn) -> REDUCED. ZnO = OXIDISING AGENT.
C: gains O (C -> CO) -> OXIDISED. C = REDUCING AGENT.

In both cases oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously = REDOX reactions.

items.question: From Activity 1.1 (burning of magnesium): identify whether Mg is oxidised or reduced. Write the equation. Is this a redox reaction? Explain.
items.answer:
Balanced equation: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s).
Analysis:
Magnesium (Mg): GAINS oxygen (Mg + O -> MgO) -> Mg is OXIDISED.
Oxygen (O2): The O2 itself is not separately reduced in the classic sense at this level; it is incorporated into MgO.

Is this a redox reaction?
YES. In this reaction:
Mg is OXIDISED (gains O).
O2 acts as OXIDISING AGENT (causes Mg to be oxidised; O atoms go from 0 valency in O2 to -2 in MgO = reduced).
This is both a combination reaction AND an oxidation reaction. The burning of magnesium ribbon with dazzling white flame in Activity 1.1 is thus also an example of oxidation.
In redox terminology: Mg = reducing agent (gets oxidised); O2 = oxidising agent (gets reduced).

items.question: Define oxidation, reduction, and redox. With three examples (equations), identify oxidised substance, reduced substance, oxidising agent, and reducing agent in each.
items.answer:
OXIDATION: Gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen. Substance is OXIDISED.
REDUCTION: Loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. Substance is REDUCED.
REDOX: Oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously in the same reaction.

EXAMPLE 1: CuO(s) + H2(g) -[Heat]-> Cu(s) + H2O(l). [Activity 1.11]
Oxidised: H2 (gains O). Reduced: CuO (loses O).
Oxidising agent: CuO. Reducing agent: H2.

EXAMPLE 2: ZnO(s) + C(s) -> Zn(s) + CO(g).
Oxidised: C (gains O, C->CO). Reduced: ZnO (loses O, ZnO->Zn).
Oxidising agent: ZnO. Reducing agent: C.
(Used in metallurgy - carbon reduces metal oxides.)

EXAMPLE 3: MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2.
Oxidised: HCl (loses H; H goes to H2O; Cl is released as Cl2).
Reduced: MnO2 (loses O, MnO2 -> MnCl2).
Oxidising agent: MnO2. Reducing agent: HCl.

items.question: In CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, which substance is reduced?
items.explanation: CuO LOSES oxygen (CuO -> Cu) = REDUCED. H2 GAINS oxygen = OXIDISED. Cu and H2O are products.

items.question: Oxidation and reduction occurring simultaneously in a reaction is called:
items.explanation: REDOX reaction = oxidation + reduction happening simultaneously. One reactant is oxidised; another is reduced at the same time. This is the definition of a redox reaction.

items.question: In Activity 1.11, when H2 is passed over heated CuO, the black coating turns brown because:

options.B: H2 reduces CuO back to copper
options.D: H2 combines with Cu to form a compound

items.explanation: CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O. H2 REDUCES CuO (removes O from CuO to form H2O). Copper metal (brown) is restored. The black CuO coating disappears.

items.question: In ZnO + C -> Zn + CO, the reducing agent is:
items.explanation: C gains O (C -> CO) = OXIDISED. The substance that gets oxidised in a redox reaction is the REDUCING AGENT (it reduces ZnO by accepting its O). ZnO is the oxidising agent (it is reduced = loses O to C).

items.question: Copper (shiny brown) on heating in air becomes black. The black compound formed is:
items.explanation: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO. Copper(II) oxide (CuO) is black. From Activity 1.11, copper powder heated in air forms black CuO. Formula is CuO (copper valency 2, oxygen valency 2; 1:1 ratio).

items.question: In MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2, the substance oxidised is:
items.explanation: HCl loses hydrogen: H goes to H2O; Cl is released as Cl2. HCl LOSES H = OXIDISED. HCl is the reducing agent. MnO2 loses O (MnO2 -> MnCl2) = REDUCED. MnO2 is the oxidising agent.

items.question: Which statement about redox reactions is CORRECT?

options.A: The oxidising agent gains oxygen and gets oxidised
options.B: The reducing agent gains oxygen and gets reduced
options.C: The oxidising agent causes reduction; itself gets reduced
options.D: Only the reducing agent changes in a redox reaction

items.explanation: OXIDISING AGENT: Causes the other substance to be oxidised (by providing O); itself GETS REDUCED (loses O). Example: CuO is oxidising agent - it oxidises H2 (H2 gains O) and CuO is reduced (loses O). Options A and B are reversed. Option D is wrong - both substances change.

topics.topic_name: HAVE YOU OBSERVED THE EFFECTS OF OXIDATION REACTIONS IN EVERYDAY LIFE?

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Oxidation reactions are not limited to laboratories - they occur around us in everyday life. Two important harmful consequences of oxidation in daily life are CORROSION of metals and RANCIDITY of fats/oils in food.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: CORROSION: Slow chemical deterioration of metals due to attack by environmental substances (moisture, O2, acids). Rusting of iron is the most common example.
RANCIDITY: Deterioration of fats/oils in food due to their oxidation by O2 in air, causing unpleasant smell and taste.
Both are OXIDATION processes and are harmful.
Prevention of corrosion: painting, galvanising, oiling, alloying (stainless steel), electroplating.
Prevention of rancidity: antioxidants, airtight containers, nitrogen flushing, refrigeration.

items.question: What is corrosion? Give two examples.
items.answer:
CORROSION is the slow chemical deterioration of a metal when it is attacked by substances in the environment like moisture, oxygen, or acids.
Examples:
(i) RUSTING of iron: Reddish-brown iron oxide (rust) forms on iron left in humid atmosphere.
(ii) TARNISHING of silver: Black silver sulphide (Ag2S) forms on silver when exposed to air.

items.question: What is rancidity? How can it be prevented?
items.answer:
RANCIDITY is the process by which fats and oils in food get oxidised when exposed to air, causing a change in their smell and taste (become unpleasant/stale).
Prevention:
(i) Adding ANTIOXIDANTS to food (prevent oxidation of fats).
(ii) Storing in AIRTIGHT containers (limits O2 contact).
(iii) FLUSHING packets with nitrogen gas (displaces O2; inert gas).

items.question: How does corrosion cause economic loss? Give three examples of structures/objects affected by corrosion.
items.answer:
Every year an enormous amount of money is spent replacing or repairing structures damaged by corrosion. Corroded metal loses strength and becomes unsafe.
Three examples:
(i) IRON BRIDGES: Corrosion (rusting) weakens iron bridges and railings; expensive repainting and replacement needed.
(ii) SHIPS: Iron hulls exposed to salt water corrode rapidly; anti-corrosion treatment is costly.
(iii) CAR BODIES: Iron/steel car bodies rust over time; expensive repairs and repainting needed.
Corrosion of iron is especially serious as iron is widely used in construction, transportation, and machinery.

items.question: Why are chips packets filled with nitrogen gas? Explain the connection with rancidity and oxidation.
items.answer:
Chips are fried in oil and their surface contains fats. If the packet contains AIR (with O2), the fats get oxidised -> RANCIDITY: unpleasant smell, bad taste.

Why NITROGEN is used:
(i) Nitrogen is an INERT gas - it does not react with fats or oils.
(ii) It DISPLACES OXYGEN from the packet.
(iii) Without O2, oxidation of fats cannot occur -> no rancidity.
(iv) Extends shelf life of the chips.

Connection to oxidation: Rancidity IS oxidation of fats. By removing O2 (replacing with N2), the oxidation reaction is prevented. The same principle applies to adding antioxidants - they prevent oxidation by reacting with O2 faster than fats do.

items.question: Explain the process of corrosion of iron. What are the conditions required for rusting? How can rusting be prevented? Give three methods.
items.answer:
CORROSION OF IRON (RUSTING):
Iron articles are shiny when new but develop a REDDISH-BROWN powdery coating when exposed to humid air. This is RUST = hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3.xH2O).

Conditions for rusting:
(i) Presence of MOISTURE (water/humidity).
(ii) Presence of OXYGEN (from air).
BOTH must be present simultaneously. Iron does not rust in dry air or in oxygen-free water.

Three methods to prevent rusting:
(i) PAINTING: Paint layer physically prevents iron from contacting O2 and moisture.
(ii) GALVANISING: Coating iron with ZINC (Zn). Zinc is more reactive - it corrodes preferentially, protecting iron. Even if zinc coat is scratched, zinc acts as sacrificial metal.
(iii) ALLOYING: Making STAINLESS STEEL (iron + chromium + nickel) - highly corrosion resistant.

items.question: Discuss harmful effects of oxidation reactions in everyday life with reference to corrosion AND rancidity. For each: describe the process, effects, and methods of prevention.
items.answer:
CORROSION:
Process: Slow oxidation of metals by environmental substances. Iron + O2 + H2O -> Fe2O3.xH2O (rust). Silver + H2S -> Ag2S (black tarnish). Copper + O2 + CO2 + H2O -> Cu2(OH)2CO3 (green verdigris).
Effects:
- Iron bridges, ships, railings, car bodies weakened and destroyed.
- Enormous money spent replacing corroded iron structures annually.
- Corroded metal unsafe to use (structural failure risk).
Prevention:
- PAINTING (physical barrier).
- GALVANISING (zinc coat - sacrificial metal).
- OILING/GREASING (for machines).
- ALLOYING (stainless steel = Fe + Cr + Ni).
- ELECTROPLATING (tin, chromium coating).

RANCIDITY:
Process: Fats and oils in food oxidised by O2 in air. Oxidation breaks fat molecules into compounds with bad smell and taste. Butter, cooking oil, fried snacks, chips become rancid.
Effects:
- Food develops unpleasant smell and bitter taste.
- Food becomes unfit for consumption.
- Reduced shelf life of packaged food products.
Prevention:
- ANTIOXIDANTS added (Vitamin E, BHA, BHT - react with O2 faster than fats, protecting them).
- AIRTIGHT CONTAINERS (reduce O2 contact).
- NITROGEN FLUSHING (inert gas displaces O2 from packets).
- REFRIGERATION (low temperature slows oxidation reaction).
- VACUUM PACKAGING (removes air from package).

COMMON FEATURE: Both corrosion and rancidity are harmful OXIDATION processes. Prevention in both cases = preventing contact with oxygen.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Rusting of iron requires:
items.explanation: Iron rusts ONLY when BOTH O2 AND moisture are present simultaneously. Dry air = no rust. Oxygen-free water = no rust. Both conditions essential.

items.question: Rancidity in food is caused by:
items.explanation: Rancidity = OXIDATION of fats/oils by O2 in air. This changes fat structure, producing unpleasant compounds. Adding antioxidants (which prevent oxidation) prevents rancidity.

items.question: Black coating on silver articles is due to:
items.explanation: Silver tarnishes due to SILVER SULPHIDE (Ag2S) formation when silver reacts with H2S traces in air. This is corrosion of silver. Ag2S is black.

items.question: Chips manufacturers flush packets with nitrogen gas to:

options.B: Increase shelf life by preventing oxidation (rancidity)
options.D: Keep chips crispy by moisture removal

items.explanation: Nitrogen (inert) displaces O2 from packets. Without O2, fats cannot be oxidised = no rancidity. Shelf life increases. Nitrogen does not add flavour, kill bacteria, or remove moisture.

items.question: Galvanising prevents rusting of iron by coating it with:
items.explanation: GALVANISING = coating iron with ZINC (Zn). Zinc is more reactive than iron; it corrodes preferentially (sacrificial protection). Even if zinc coat scratches, it protects iron underneath.

items.question: Antioxidants added to food prevent rancidity by:
items.explanation: ANTIOXIDANTS prevent OXIDATION of fats. They react with O2 faster than fats do, scavenging O2 before it oxidises fats. This prevents rancidity. Examples: Vitamin E, BHA, BHT.

items.question: Green coating on copper vessels exposed to air is:
items.explanation: Verdigris = basic copper carbonate Cu2(OH)2CO3 (or CuCO3.Cu(OH)2). Forms when copper reacts with O2 + CO2 + H2O in air. This is corrosion of copper. CuO is black, CuS is dark, Cu(NO3)2 is the salt not surface coating.

items.question: To prevent rancidity in butter, which TWO actions together are MOST effective?

options.A: Store in transparent jar + keep in sunlight
options.B: Store in airtight container + add antioxidant
options.C: Wrap loosely in paper + keep at room temperature
options.D: Add water to butter + store open

items.explanation: Rancidity = oxidation of fats by O2. Airtight container prevents O2 contact; antioxidant further inhibits oxidation reaction. This dual action is MOST effective. Option A - sunlight accelerates photo-oxidation. Option C - paper is permeable to air. Option D - water promotes bacterial growth.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: CORROSION is the process by which metals are slowly eaten away (deteriorated) due to chemical attack by substances in the environment such as moisture, oxygen, and acids. The metal surface reacts with these substances to form oxides, sulphides, or carbonates.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: RUSTING: Corrosion of iron. Rust = hydrated iron(III) oxide Fe2O3.xH2O. Reddish-brown, flaky, powdery.
Conditions for rusting: BOTH moisture AND oxygen must be present.
TARNISHING of silver: Ag + H2S -> Ag2S (black). Corrosion of silver.
GREEN COATING on copper: Basic copper carbonate (verdigris) - corrosion of copper.
Corrosion weakens metal structures; enormous economic loss annually.
Prevention methods: PAINTING, GALVANISING (zinc coat), OILING/GREASING, ELECTROPLATING, ALLOYING (stainless steel = Fe + Cr + Ni).
STAINLESS STEEL (Fe + Cr + Ni) is highly corrosion resistant - used in cutlery, surgical instruments.

items.question: What is corrosion? Why is rusting of iron a serious problem?
items.answer:
CORROSION is the slow deterioration of metals due to attack by moisture, oxygen, and other environmental substances.
Rusting is serious because: iron is very widely used in construction (bridges, buildings), transportation (ships, vehicles), and machinery. Rusting weakens iron, making structures unsafe. Enormous amounts of money are spent yearly replacing or repairing rusted iron structures.

items.question: What is rusting? What conditions are required for rusting? Give three methods to prevent it.
items.answer:
RUSTING: Corrosion of iron in which a reddish-brown, flaky layer of hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3.xH2O) forms on iron's surface when exposed to moist air.
Conditions: BOTH oxygen AND moisture must be present simultaneously.
Three prevention methods:
(i) PAINTING: Paint layer keeps O2 and moisture away from iron.
(ii) GALVANISING: Coat with zinc (Zn). Zinc more reactive - corrodes preferentially (sacrificial protection).
(iii) ALLOYING: Stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni) - inherently rust resistant.

items.question: Explain galvanising as a method to prevent rusting. Why does zinc protect iron even when the zinc coat is scratched?
items.answer:
GALVANISING: Iron/steel is coated with a thin layer of ZINC metal (by hot-dipping or electroplating).

How it works:
(i) As long as zinc coat is INTACT: Zinc forms a physical barrier preventing iron from contacting O2/moisture.
(ii) Even if zinc coat is SCRATCHED: Zinc is MORE REACTIVE than iron in the reactivity series. When O2 and moisture attack, zinc reacts preferentially (zinc corrodes, not iron). Zinc acts as SACRIFICIAL METAL - it sacrifices itself to protect iron.
(iii) Iron beneath remains protected until all zinc is consumed.

Economic advantage: Galvanised iron lasts much longer than plain iron. Used for iron pipes, roofing sheets, buckets, wires.

Painting, by contrast, works ONLY as a physical barrier. Once paint is scratched, iron underneath is exposed and rusts rapidly. Galvanising provides both physical and electrochemical protection.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Rusting is corrosion of which metal?
items.explanation: RUSTING specifically = corrosion of IRON/STEEL. Product = hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust). Copper corrosion = green verdigris. Silver corrosion = black Ag2S (tarnish).

items.question: Coating iron with zinc to prevent rusting is called:
items.explanation: GALVANISING = coating iron with ZINC (Zn). Tinning = tin coat. Electroplating = electric current used for metal coating. Alloying = mixing metals (e.g., stainless steel).

items.question: Conditions required for rusting of iron are:
items.explanation: Iron kept in completely dry air does NOT rust. Iron submerged in oxygen-free water does NOT rust. BOTH moisture AND oxygen must be present at the same time for rusting to occur.

items.question: Oil or grease is applied to iron tools to prevent corrosion because:

options.A: Oil reacts with oxygen to stop rusting
options.B: Oil forms a barrier preventing contact with air and moisture
options.D: Oil coats iron with a reactive metal

items.explanation: Oil/grease forms a PHYSICAL BARRIER on iron surface, preventing direct contact with O2 and moisture. Without contact, corrosion cannot occur. Same principle as painting. Oil does not react with O2.

items.question: Stainless steel is composed of:
items.explanation: STAINLESS STEEL = Iron + Chromium + Nickel (+ small amount of carbon). Chromium forms a thin protective Cr2O3 layer on surface, making it corrosion resistant. Used for cutlery, surgical instruments, kitchen utensils.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: RANCIDITY is the deterioration of fats and oils in food materials due to their OXIDATION by oxygen in air. Rancid food has an unpleasant smell and bitter/bad taste and is unfit for consumption.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Fats/oils are oxidised by O2 -> new compounds with bad smell/taste formed = rancidity.
Signs of rancidity: unpleasant smell, bitter/sour taste, sometimes colour change.
ANTIOXIDANTS: Substances added to food to prevent oxidation of fats. Examples: Vitamin E (tocopherol), BHA (butylated hydroxyanisole).
AIRTIGHT CONTAINERS: Reduce O2 contact -> slow down oxidation.
NITROGEN FLUSHING: Inert N2 displaces O2 from packets of chips/snacks -> no oxidation possible.
REFRIGERATION: Low temperature slows oxidation rate.
VACUUM PACKAGING: Removes air (and O2) from package.
Usually substances which prevent oxidation (antioxidants) are added to foods containing fats.

items.question: Why do chips manufacturers flush bags with nitrogen gas?
items.answer:
Chips contain fat on their surface. If packets contain air (O2), fats get OXIDISED causing RANCIDITY - chips smell bad and taste stale.
Nitrogen is used because:
(i) N2 is INERT - does not react with fats.
(ii) It DISPLACES O2 from the packet.
Without O2, no oxidation = no rancidity. Shelf life is extended.

items.question: What is rancidity? Describe its signs. Give three methods to prevent rancidity.
items.answer:
RANCIDITY: Deterioration of fats and oils in food due to their oxidation by O2, leading to unpleasant smell and taste.
Signs: (i) Unpleasant/bad smell (different from fresh food). (ii) Bitter or sour taste. (iii) Possible colour change.

Three methods to prevent:
(i) ANTIOXIDANTS: Added to packaged food (Vitamin E, BHA, BHT). They react with O2 faster than fats do, protecting fats from oxidation.
(ii) AIRTIGHT PACKAGING: Sealed airtight containers reduce O2 contact with food, slowing oxidation.
(iii) NITROGEN FLUSHING: Packets flushed with N2 before sealing. N2 is inert, displaces O2, prevents fat oxidation.

items.question: Explain the relationship between oxidation and rancidity. Why are antioxidants added to fat-containing foods? Give two examples of antioxidants.
items.answer:
RELATIONSHIP: Rancidity IS CAUSED BY oxidation of fats. When food containing fats/oils is exposed to O2 in air, the fat molecules are oxidised. This oxidation breaks down fat structure, forming compounds with unpleasant smell and bitter taste. Since rancidity = oxidation, any measure that prevents oxidation prevents rancidity.

Why ANTIOXIDANTS are added:
Antioxidants prevent or inhibit oxidation of fats by:
(i) Reacting with O2 FASTER than fats do (scavenging O2 before it oxidises fats).
(ii) Breaking the chain reaction of fat oxidation.
This significantly extends the shelf life of fat-containing foods (butter, chips, edible oils, packaged snacks) while keeping their smell and taste pleasant.

Two examples of antioxidants:
(i) VITAMIN E (tocopherol): Natural antioxidant present in vegetable oils; also added to food products.
(ii) BHA (Butylated Hydroxyanisole): Synthetic antioxidant added to chips, butter, cereals to prevent rancidity.

items.question: Rancidity is caused by:
items.explanation: Rancidity = OXIDATION of fats/oils by O2 in air. This changes fat structure producing bad smell and taste. Adding antioxidants (which prevent oxidation) is the key prevention method.

items.question: Antioxidants are added to food to:
items.explanation: ANTIOXIDANTS prevent OXIDATION of fats/oils in food, thereby preventing rancidity and extending shelf life. They do not add flavour, increase fat, or kill bacteria.

items.question: Which of the following does NOT prevent rancidity?

options.C: Storing in transparent jars in sunlight

items.explanation: Storing in sunlight ACCELERATES rancidity (sunlight provides energy that speeds up photo-oxidation of fats). Options A, B, D all reduce O2 contact or inhibit oxidation, thus preventing rancidity.

items.question: Smell of rancid butter is due to:

options.B: Formation of new compounds by oxidation of fats

items.explanation: When butter becomes rancid, fats are OXIDISED. Oxidation forms new compounds (free fatty acids, aldehydes, ketones) with unpleasant odour. Fresh butter's pleasant smell is replaced by rancid odour.

items.question: Two butter samples A (with antioxidant BHA added) and B (no antioxidant) stored identically. After 10 days only B becomes rancid. This shows:

options.B: BHA prevented oxidation of fats in A

items.explanation: The ONLY difference = BHA added to A. B became rancid (fats oxidised) but A did not. Therefore BHA in A PREVENTED OXIDATION of fats. This demonstrates the effectiveness of antioxidants in preventing rancidity. Conditions were identical, so temperature is not the cause.
